stories.title: Over 30 women allege harassment and misogyny in ambulance service
stories.summary: An unpublished Health Service Executive (HSE) internal review obtained by the programme also raised concerns about the culture and leadership of the service, including references to bullying and harassment and what it described as a traditional "command and control" management style. The report, carried out by the HSE's Workplace Health and Wellbeing Unit, has not previously been published or reported on. Documents obtained by Prime Time also show that concerns about misogyny, gender discrimination and sexual harassment were raised with the Director of the NAS Robert Morton by senior management. The women who spoke to the programme include current and former paramedics and emergency medical technicians. Many spoke anonymously because they continue to work in the service. They stressed that there are many good people working within NAS, including many men, but described what they believe is a long-standing culture in which inappropriate behaviour was tolerated and complaints were not always properly addressed. NAS is a part of the HSE in which more than 2,400 staff are employed nationwide.

stories.title: Parents felt 'abandoned' over lack of special school supports
stories.summary: Parents of children at some Community Special Schools have criticised gaps in staffing and resources which they say have resulted in children with special educational needs regressing or being hurt at school. In response to the increased demand for places, the Government has been expanding the Community Special School (CSS) model, with the schools run by local Education and Training Boards (ETBs) and catering for children with intellectual disabilities and complex needs. There are currently 15 CSSs around the country – the first opened in 2019 - with three more due to open this school year. However, parents who spoke to Prime Time say the specialist staffing and supports required by their children have not kept pace with the creation of new school places. Louise O'Keeffe says her 13-year-old daughter Ella, who has an intellectual disability and autism, lost "hours and hours of progression" after she began attending Belmayne Community Special School in Dublin 13 last year. The school was due to open in August 2025, but it did not begin operating until November. It then opened on reduced hours before gradually increasing to three and a half hours, while some students attended for even less time.

stories.title: Burnham commits to Good Friday Agreement on border poll
stories.summary: British Prime Minster Andy Burnham has said he will "stick to the Good Friday Agreement 100%", including on the matter of holding a referendum on re-unification. He was replying to Scottish National Party MP Chris Law, who asked if it was right that Northern Ireland has a mechanism for a referendum set out in law, but Scotland does not. "I would also remind him on that question of a border poll: it is to be considered by the Northern Ireland Secretary when there is a clear consensus in the country, when public opinion has changed to the point where the call has to be considered," Mr Burnham said. "I would say exactly the same situation in Scotland. I am not aware that there is a majority of public support for another referendum, and until that changes, Mr Speaker, there won't be one." Mr Burham received criticism last month when he told the media in Belfast that a referendum on a united Ireland was "off the table". He made the remarks when asked about the prospects of a border poll on his first official visit to Northern Ireland as British Prime Minister.

stories.title: Brent holds above $100 as tanker attacks dampen hopes
stories.summary: Oil prices rose today, extending gains that took Brent over $100 a barrel in the previous session, as traders braced for deeper supply disruptions after Iran and the US launched their largest attacks on shipping since their six-month-old conflict began. Brent crude futures were up by 40 cents, or 0.4%, at $101.61 a barrel this morning. US West Texas Intermediate crude rose by 49 cents, or 0.51%, to $96.54. Brent prices have surged nearly 30% from lows touched in early August as a permanent agreement between the US and Iran to cease attacks never materialised and fighting resumed later in the month. "The recent run-up in prices lays bare the market's approach: this conflict will last longer than anticipated even a month ago, let alone at the beginning of the summer. If oil supply and exports are diminished, the oil balance remains tight and prices remain elevated," PVM analyst John Evans said. US President Donald Trump warned that the US may hit Iran's Pickaxe Mountain, urging Tehran to be cautious, and said that the war will likely last beyond the November midterm elections. Iran said it had attacked 10 ships near the Strait of Hormuz yesterday, after the US sank five Iranian oil tankers. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it would escalate its response to any further attacks.

stories.title: Oslo falls silent for funeral of Norway's King Harald V
stories.summary: Norway's King Harald V has been laid to rest, marking the end of 13 days of national mourning following his death at the age of 89. He was a reformer who spent more than three decades on the throne, after gradually emerging from the shadow of his popular and charismatic father, and died at a time of multiple crises for the Norwegian royal family. A procession on foot from the royal palace to Oslo Cathedral started at 12pm (11am Irish time), punctuated by the sound of cannons being fired from the city's Akershus Fortress. Tens of thousands of people lined the capital's Karl Johan Avenue, police said, with crowds falling silent as the coffin passed. The procession was followed by a church ceremony, beginning with a nationwide minute of silence. Among the mourners were President Catherine Connolly, Britain's Prince William and Princess Anne; Japan's Crown Prince Akishino and Crown Princess Kiko; Spain's King Felipe, Queen Letizia and Queen Sofia; Sweden's royal family; and Denmark's King Frederik and Queen Mary.

stories.title: GAA rejects misogyny accusations after McAleese quits
stories.summary: GAA director general Tom Ryan has rejected accusations of misogyny "in the strongest possible terms" after it was revealed the integration of Gaelic games' three bodies will not happen in 2027. Ryan said a failure to reach agreement on "organisational structures" is the main reason behind the delay in the process. Dr Mary McAleese, the former President of Ireland, yesterday stood down as chairperson of the Integration Committee overseeing the amalgamation of the GAA, LGFA and Camogie Association. McAleese cited changes to agreed timelines, a GAA management committee that she described as "less than impressive", and her feeling that there were "people who are not entirely happy about the idea of including women in decision-making at the top level of Gaelic sports" who were holding the process back. "I can't accept that, I would refute that in the strongest possible terms," Ryan said when asked about accusations that the delays are built on misogyny. "I accept in the course of a project like this, there will be different perspectives and different points of view, and that's fine.

stories.title: Parrott marks Champions League debut with Betis winner
stories.summary: Troy Parrott marked his Champions League debut with a goal as Real Betis earned a 3-2 win at ten-man Lille. Only four days after netting his first Betis goal - a home winner against Real Madrid in La Liga - the Republic of Ireland striker was at it again, scoring what proved to be the winning goal eight minutes after half-time. Betis defender Marc Bartra had scored twice either side of half-time to cancel out goals from Ayase Ueda and Alexsandro Ribeiro before Parrott pounced. With the scores locked at 2-2, the Dubliner latched onto a through ball from Rodrigo Riquelme, made space for himself in the Lille box, before firing a low shot beyond the outstretched leg of Berke Ozer. Three minutes later, Ethan Mbappe, brother of Real Madrid and France striker Kylian, was sent off for Lille with Betis holding out for victory on their return to the Champions League stage after two decades. Parrott started the opening league phase game of this season's competition at the Stade Pierre-Mauroy and played the full 90 minutes plus stoppage time.

stories.title: Round up: Ulster and Connacht bag first pre-season wins
stories.summary: Ulster and Connacht recorded their first pre-season victories in two tense tussles over the weekend. On Friday night, Richie Murphy's Ulster scraped past fellow URC challengers Edinburgh in Scotland, three weeks prior to their opening league clash on 25 September. As for Connacht, they were big winners over English CHAMP side Ealing Trailfinders, whose squad featured four Irish players. Ulster got their pre-season campaign off to an ideal start with a narrow two-point victory over Edinburgh in the Hive Stadium on Friday night. Debutant half-backs Jamie Benson and Matthew Devine combined for 11 points, with the former Connacht man scoring a first-half try, as Ulster raced into a 14 point lead after just 25 minutes. With a 27-man travelling squad named by Richie Murphy, all eyes were on the plentiful supply of new faces. Benson and Devine combined at half-back, Daniel Hawkshaw and Chay Mullins also started in the backline with Eduardo Bello, Ben Donnell, Eli Snyman and Martin Moloney all among the replacements. Academy prospects Flynn Longstaff and Jed Findlay rounded off the debutants from the bench also. The visitors raced into an early lead helped by set-piece dominance. A scrum penalty win led to the first try, with hooker James McCormick dotting down from the back of a powerful rolling maul. Edinburgh responded with a try of their own courtesy of centre Geordie Gwynn, but then came Ulster's gear change.

stories.title: Something for the Weekend: Roisin Kiberd's cultural picks
stories.summary: In her new collection of essays The Most Normal Woman, critically acclaimed author Roisin Kiberd explores the many ways we change ourselves in pursuit of perfection – or simply normality – and the toll it takes on our inner lives. Weaving critical commentary with personal experience, she explores Botox, blondeness, exercise addiction, and subcultures including the underground drag scene and competitive dog shows to better understand how beauty is judged and defined. Last year I entered an intense Kaiju film phase. Before that I didn't understand monster films – the human story barely seems to matter in them, only the monster smashing up a city – but something inspired me to watch the original Godzilla, and there was a moment when it suddenly clicked: the monster is the star of the show. Its rampage provides us with catharsis, the rush of absolute destruction. Now I’m kaiju-obsessed. I especially loved the 1961 film Gorgo, which was made in England, with some scenes shot in Ireland too. Gorgo, the monster, emerges from Coliemore Harbour in Dalkey. I’ve been on walks there since and always want to call out to the water and see if he’ll appear. When I’m working I mostly listen to ambient music like Aphex Twin, Brian Eno and Harold Budd, who Rob, my partner, introduced me to. But lately we’ve also been playing old Beck albums in the car, and it feels really beautiful to rediscover an artist I loved when I was in college, but with someone else this time, finding out where our favourites overlap and differ. Esther Yi’s Y/N, an eerie, hypnotic study of K-pop fandom and identity collapse, was one of my favourite books in recent years, and her follow-up, a short story collection titled To God, will be out later this year. I’m also looking forward to reading Switzy by Emma Cline. Her last novel, The Guest, was one I returned to several times, trying to deconstruct it and work out what made it so stressful, in the best possible way.

stories.title: Harry Styles fuels Irish gig hopes with 2027 tease
stories.summary: Harry Styles has fuelled hopes of a return to Ireland after posters linked to the singer appeared in Dublin as he prepares to reveal the final cities on his Together, Together tour. The former One Direction star teased the announcement overnight with a cryptic Instagram post captioned: "2027. Tomorrow." It follows days of speculation after colourful posters carrying the date 10.09.26 appeared around Dublin, with similar artwork spotted in cities including Rome, Berlin, Madrid, Los Angeles and Toronto. The imagery has been linked to Styles' recent "Snail Mail" campaign, prompting fans to connect the Dublin posters with the singer ahead of Thursday’s announcement. Styles has now confirmed in an email to fans that new dates will be added to his Together, Together tour in 2027. "When we decided to do the 2026 tour I knew it would be special but what you turned it into was far beyond what I could have imagined," he wrote.

stories.title: Dutch to fine Irish carriers transporting unweaned calves
stories.summary: The Dutch Food and Safety Authority (NVWA) has announced that it will impose fines on four Irish carriers transporting unweaned calves to the Netherlands. The move is in response to claims the animals are not fed during the sea crossing, even though they are legally required to be fed during transport. The Netherlands is a key destination for Irish dairy calves sold to mainland Europe, with around 200,000 animals leaving the country every year. They are mostly used for veal production, and are usually transported via sea from Ireland to France, before making the rest of the journey via road. Animal welfare groups claim this situation can lead to calves becoming weak, suffering from dehydration and hypoglycaemia, and even dying en route. It is understood that Irish transporters bringing calves to the Netherlands will initially be given a warning and 12 months to find a more "humane and animal-friendly manner" in which to move them.

stories.title: Fórsa health workers to take industrial action this month
stories.summary: Members of the Fórsa trade union working in the public health sector are to begin industrial action later this month over delays in agreeing a new public sector pay deal. The union has issued formal notice of industrial action to employers in the health sector, including the HSE, Tusla and Section 38 organisations. Industrial action will begin on Wednesday 30 September and will initially take the form of a work-to-rule. Staff will refuse to do overtime, cover duties attached to vacant posts, and cooperate with proposals to extend working patterns across a seven-day roster. Last week, members of Fórsa in the public sector voted overwhelmingly in favour of taking industrial action. So too have several other public sector unions over what they describe as the Government's failure to make a meaningful offer on public sector pay.

stories.title: Glenveagh Properties H1 profits and revenues sink
stories.summary: Homebuilder Glenveagh Properties has reported a sharp drop in half year profits and revenues but said it was upgrading its total home completion guidance for the year to more than 2,900 units. Glenveagh's after tax profits for the six months to the end of June slumped by 97% to €1m from €32.5m, while its revenues sank 30% to €239.7m from €341.6m. Glenveagh said its average selling price rose to about €402,000 from €377,000 the same time last year due to the higher proportion of non-standard homes on portions of sites bought in late 2024 where planning was secured by previous owners. Average selling prices are expected to be approximately €380,000 for 2026. The company said it now expects to complete more than 2,900 units in 2026, up from it earlier guidance of 2,750. This inclues over 1,700 units (up from 1,600) in its Homebuilding division and about 1,200 units (previously 1,150) in its Partnerships business division. It added that its combined 2026 and 2027 homebuilding deliveries remains at approximately 3,600 units.

stories.title: Minister expects integration congresses to happen in 2027
stories.summary: Minister for Sport Patrick O'Donovan says he doesn't expect there to be a long delay to the integration of all three Gaelic games bodies in the wake of Mary McAleese's resignation from the integration committee earlier this week. McAleese stepped away as the chairperson of the committee on Tuesday, a move which O'Donovan said was "really disappointing." The Minister met separately McAleese, as well as representatives from the GAA, the LGFA and the Camogie Association on Wednesday to get a sense of where the process was at, and he said that he expects integration to happen sooner rather than later. "This is the largest change in Gaelic Games administration since the foundation of the GAA in Hayes Hotel in 1884. The one thing is all of the bodies are signed up to it. "I asked a very straight question of all three of them yesterday - 'are you signed up to integration, a fully integrated single Gaelic Games organisation?' Special Congresses of the three Gaelic games bodies, which were planned for October, will not take place as final details around integration remain to be worked out.

stories.title: New hurling amendments to be trialled in Fitzgibbon Cup
stories.summary: A series of hurling rule amendments are set for use in the Fitzgibbon Cup league games, on recommendation from the GAA's hurling expert advisory group. The main amendments will see the banning of two consecutive hand-passes – a free being awarded to the opposition from the point where the second hand-pass was attempted – and an increase to six steps allowed for players in possession. Hand-passes, meanwhile, will also now require a "clear and definite striking action of a hand" - with "clear" added to the previous "definite striking action" rule wording. Line umpires will be given stronger power to act on indiscretions while players contesting throw-ins must clash with a ground stroke and failure to do so will result in a free to the opposition. All other players are required to remain 13 metres back. Puck-outs must also cross the 45-metre line before being played by the defending team while '65s’ will now move back to be taken from the 65m-line in the opposition half. Sideline cuts that go over the bar without a touch from another attacking player will be worth two points.

stories.title: Maresca 'didn't see nothing' in tetchy Porto affair
stories.summary: Enzo Maresca shed little light on the tunnel bust-up that overshadowed Manchester City's opening Champions League win against Porto. Players from both sides were involved in scuffles as they headed down the tunnel at half-time of City’s niggly 2-0 victory at the Estadio do Dragao on Tuesday. Porto had felt City’s Marc Guehi should have been sent off after catching Gabri Veiga with his arm as he jumped for a header. That led to arguments on the field and tempers had not cooled by the time the half-time whistle blew. There were reports of pushing between players and some footage appeared to show City captain Ruben Dias putting his hand on Porto coach Francesco Farioli’s chest. City manager Maresca said he "didn’t see nothing" when asked about the Guehi incident and was already in the dressing room when the half-time incident unfolded.

stories.title: Refreshed Van der Flier ready for World Cup year
stories.summary: Leinster and Ireland flanker Josh van der Flier knows that nothing is won in early September, but that doesn't mean that the 2027 Rugby World Cup escapes the imagination ahead of the start of the 2026/27 season. Speaking at the launch of the IRFU’s new men’s and women’s national team jerseys at the Guinness Open Gate Brewery this week, the 33-year-old was in fine form, which could be attributed to a healthy body and mind. "(I’m) feeling fit as well and getting back into a bit of pre-season stuff and ready for a big few months." This optimistic outlook will come as soothing words to head coach Andy Farrell, who prepares his 12-month plan where all roads hopefully lead to a World Cup final in Sydney on Saturday, 13 November. Van der Flier was part of the two most recent touring squads to Japan in 2019 and France in 2023, where both Irish efforts were ended by the All Blacks. There is a feeling of now or never ahead of the next edition however, but van der Flier insists that he is taking the coming months one at a time. "It's always tempting to start thinking of those (major tournaments), but it's obviously like how rugby goes, it tends to be week-to-week and you've got to look after your pre-season first," he said.

stories.title: 5 autumn trends you can actually wear to work
stories.summary: As office dress codes have relaxed, there’s more scope for personality, but translating the season’s more adventurous trends into something suitable for a Monday morning can still be tricky. "I think the interesting thing with workwear now is that people want to feel current without looking as though they’ve just copied a trend from [Instagram]," says fashion stylist Oriona Robb, "and that balance is really important." But Instagram and TikTok’s workwear inspiration, often dubbed as ‘office siren’, is far from the reality of dressing appropriately for the office. So here’s how to actually translate autumn trends into workwear. After spending the summer pairing capris with ballet flats and flatform sandals, capri pants aren't disappearing just because temperatures are dropping. The cropped silhouette actually translates perfectly into autumn and workwear – but Robb says you need to get the fabric and fit right. "I think they can absolutely work for the office […] I would always choose something tailored and structured rather than anything too tight or casual – so no prints or denim."

stories.title: Trump offers Americans $5,000 if Republicans win Congress
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump said he would pay every American adult a $5,000 (€4,299) "Trump dividend" if Republicans retain control of Congress in November's midterm election, a striking attempt to persuade voters to back his party. Mr Trump made the proposal at his Republican Party's first-ever midterm convention, but it was not immediately clear how the payments would work or whether they would be legal. With approximately 270 million US adults, the idea would cost around $1.35 trillion. During his primetime address, Mr Trump boasted of completing "the greatest two years in the history of the presidency," putting himself squarely at the center of the election despite his deepening unpopularity. But it was not clear whether his campaign-style speech would appeal to the critical swing voters who opinion polls show have drifted away from Mr Trump's party, amid growing dissatisfaction with the cost of living and the war on Iran. "We hand America's future to the radical left Democrats, and our nation will spend the next decade just getting back on its feet," he said.

stories.summary: Children's Health Ireland (CHI) is looking to challenge the perception that palliative care is only about end of life care. Music therapy is one of the ways it is providing emotional, social and spiritual support to patients, alongside medical care. Eight-year-old Rueben Fay attends CHI in Temple Street in Dublin for music therapy, with music therapist Dr James Burns. Reuben has Cerebral Palsy and multiple complex needs, and his mother Nikita is his full time carer as he lives with this life-limiting condition. Ms Fay said Reuben is a happy boy and day to day life is 24-hour care.

stories.title: Further fuel price measures may be needed, says Taoiseach
stories.summary: Taoiseach Micheál Martin has intimated there may be a need for further measures to help combat the rising prices of petrol and diesel. The Fianna Fáil leader was speaking on the second day of his party's annual think-in Tullamore after the lobby group Fuels for Ireland last week claimed diesel prices had risen to about €2 a litre in some forecourts. Mr Martin refused to rule out a further subsidy for fuel after the Coalition last month moved to extend excise cuts - introduced in the Spring - until November amid the ongoing blockage of the Strait of Hormuz with no resolution to the US-Iran war in sight. "We have to look at that and we are discussing that in the next two to three weeks in terms of the overall picture. "That’s notwithstanding if there was a breakthrough in talks between the United States and Iran and the Middle East more generally. So, we have to factor all of that that in." The Cork South Central TD rejected an assertion he had given in to the demands of April’s fuel protesters or that he had prioritised their demands over doing more to help people with rising household bills.

stories.title: What's involved in the fight against money laundering in Ireland?
stories.summary: Analysis: Criminal gangs are increasingly using technology, international financial networks and sophisticated corporate structures to move their money The recent case involving Francisco de Borbon, a distant cousin of Spain's King Felipe VI and a director of a Dublin-registered fintech company, reads almost like the script of a crime thriller. Spanish investigators have alleged links between De Borbon, an Irish fintech, an international drug-trafficking network and financial structures used to move suspected proceeds of cocaine trafficking. De Borbon was arrested in Spain in February and subsequently released on bail; he has denied wrongdoing and said he never intended to be a director of the Irish company. The significance of the story for Ireland is not that an aristocrat happens to feature in a criminal investigation or that the existence of an Irish-registered company, by itself, establishes wrongdoing in Ireland. Its broader significance lies in what it illustrates about the nature of contemporary financial crime: criminal networks are far more sophisticated, multidisciplinary and pervasive than we might assume. Over the past decade, Ireland has become one of the world's most important centres for both investment funds and money market funds. The scale is extraordinary. PwC's 2026 asset and wealth management review estimates that assets under management in Ireland could reach US$9 trillion by 2030. Ireland already domiciles approximately 75% of Europe's exchange-traded fund (ETF) market, while European assets under management are projected to increase from $35 trillion in 2024 to $48.5 trillion by 2030. Such volumes change the nature of the risk. For Ireland, these represent enormous economic opportunities and equally important risks, as well as public-policy responsibilities. Investment funds are not inherently suspicious and perform essential economic functions.The problem is that the same characteristics that make these structures economically attractive - large transaction volumes, cross-border activity, professional intermediaries, complex ownership chains and highly mobile capital - can also make them attractive to organised financial criminals.

stories.title: Russian strike on Ukraine-Moldova border kills two
stories.summary: Two civilians were killed in a Russian drone strike at a checkpoint on Ukraine's border with Moldova, the regional governor said. "Tonight, enemy drones attacked the Starokozache international road checkpoint on the border with Moldova," Odesa regional governor Oleg Kiper wrote on social media. "Sadly, there are casualties among the civilians who were near the checkpoint: according to preliminary information, two people were killed and three wounded." An image attached to Mr Kiper's message showed a deserted border post littered with debris. The attack forced the closure of the checkpoint, around 500km south of Kyiv, Ukraine's State Border Guard Service said. A Moldovan driver was also injured in the attack, according to the country's foreign ministry.

stories.title: Hansen hails Lancaster as Connacht target silverware
stories.summary: Connacht back Mack Hansen has paid tribute to the early groundwork Stuart Lancaster has done at the province, as they target silverware in the upcoming 2026/27 season. The Ireland and Lions star only featured once for his province last year due to a series of injuries, but now in year two of the Lancaster project, the focus is on further progression following a return to the URC play-offs last year. Speaking at the launch of Canterbury's new Speed Falcon 2.0 boot designed by Hansen, the 28-year-old was effusive in where he believes the men from the west are heading. "We're going for silverware and we're going to win something", he told reporters on Wednesday. "It's a great feeling around the place and we're all on the same page for that." Connacht finished in eighth place in the URC last season, losing in the quarter-final stages away to Glasgow Warriors. They also suffered quarter-final elimination in the EPCR Challenge Cup where they were dispatched by eventual champions Montpellier.
